exercise_1.title: Exercise #1
exercise_1.visible_parameters: Valider/ modifier les éléments qui apparaissent en vous référant à l'écran (Data, output, features, colorscale, weight)

instructions.text: Adjust the model parameters to classify the Gaussian dataset. Monitor how each change impacts your results. Once the classification is good enough, you will progress to two activities that validate this exercise. First, hover over parameters to view their definitions.

exercise_1.start_marker: Let's Start! Use the slider to change the weight of the features X1 and X2 to find out if your dataset can be classified.
exercise_1.target_achieved: Great job! Your settings lead to a good classification of our data into two clusters. Let's review together what you've learned from this exercise

data.definition: Numeric values that the model aims to classify

output.definition: The output is the result produced by the model, showing its classification based on the input data and the choice of parameters. The background colors represent the model's decision: blue for one group, orange for the other, and the border between them is the decision boundary.

x_axis.definition: Each axis shows the range of synthetic values that an input can take, on an arbitrary scale from -6 to +6.

y_axis.definition: Each axis shows the range of synthetic values that an input can take, on an arbitrary scale from -6 to +6.

color_scale.definition: Colors show the model's confidence: blue means the model predicts one group, orange the other. Strong colors mean high confidence; lighter colors mean uncertainty.

features.definition: A feature is a measurable property or characteristic used as input for a machine learning model. For example, in a house price prediction model, features might include size, location, number of rooms, and age of the house.

weight.definition:
A weight is a value that controls how much an input influences the output.
During training, the model adjusts the weights to reduce its prediction errors.
In a neural network the weight determines the strength or importance of a connection between neurons

qcm.question: How did you adjust the weights of X1 and X2 to get a good classification?

options.text: X1 had to be lower than X2
options.feedback: Not quite. Both inputs are equally important to separate the plan in the diagonal orientation of these specific clusters.
Random selection is not a deterministic strategy. A proper ratio must be found.

options.text: X1 and X2 had to be equivalent
options.feedback: You got it! X1 and X2 must have similar or equivalent weights to position the decision boundary at a 45-degree angle, perfectly separating the clusters.

options.text: X1 had to be bigger than X2
options.feedback: Not quite. If X1 is significantly larger, the slope of the line will lean too much towards one axis.

statements.statement: A neural network works as a linear classifier.
statements.feedback: A neural network without hidden layers behaves like a linear model. It becomes non-linear only when hidden layers and activation functions are added.

statements.statement: A simple logistic classification can only separate data that is linearly separable.
statements.feedback: Logistic regression creates a straight decision boundary. It can only work when the classes can be separated by a straight line (or hyperplane).

statements.statement: Hidden layers are necessary to classify a linear binary dataset
statements.feedback: Hidden layers are not required for linear binary classification because the problem can be solved entirely using a linear model. They become necessary only when the dataset is non-linear.

statements.statement: If a dataset has two clusters, it is always possible to draw a straight boundary between them.
statements.feedback: Even if a dataset has only two clusters, their shape and position matter. If the clusters are arranged in a curved or interleaved way (for example circles or moons), no straight line can separate them without making errors. A straight boundary works only when the clusters are linearly separable.

exercise_2.title: Exercise #2

instructions.text:
Launch the training of the neural network using the step-by-step button and observe how the weighs change and the loss decreases over time. Once training is complete, we will walk through the training process step by step.

First, hover over parameters to view their definitions.

exercise_2.start_marker:
Ready to start the training?
Go!
exercise_2.target_achieved: Great! The model has successfully learned to classify the data. Now let's go back and review the different training steps.

tooltips.epoch: An epoch is one complete pass of the entire training dataset through a machine learning model during the training process. Training usually requires multiple epochs so the model can gradually improve its predictions.
tooltips.training_loss: Training Loss measures how wrong the model's predictions are on the training data. During training, this value decreases as the model learns
tooltips.training_loss_more_info: Training loss is a numerical measure of the error between the model's predictions and the expected outputs on the training data.
tooltips.gradient_descent: Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm that updates the model's parameters step by step to reduce the loss.

explanations.title: Step 0 – Initial parameters are set
explanations.description: Before training begins, the neural network’s basic parameters (such as weights and bias) are automatically initialized. These initial values are usually small and random, allowing the model to start making predictions even before learning begins.

explanations.title: Step 1 – Training starts
explanations.description: The training process is launched. From this point on, the model repeatedly processes the training data in order to improve its predictions.

explanations.title: Step 2 – The epoch counter records the first pass
explanations.description: The epoch counter displays the first epoch, indicating that the model is starting its first complete pass through the training dataset. An epoch represents one full cycle in which all training examples are seen by the model once.

explanations.title: Step 3 – The training loss is calculated
explanations.description: After making predictions using the current parameters, the model computes the training loss. This value measures the difference between the model's predictions and the expected outputs, providing a numerical indication of how wrong the model currently is.

explanations.title: Step 4 – Gradient descent updates the parameters
explanations.description: The gradient descent algorithm uses the training loss to compute how the model's parameters should be adjusted. It updates the weights and bias in a direction that reduces the loss, improving the model's predictions.

explanations.title: Step 5 – A new training step begins
explanations.description: With the updated parameters, the model starts a new training step. This cycle—prediction, loss calculation, and parameter update—is repeated over many steps and epochs until the loss stabilizes.

statements.statement: The model already exhibits a decision boundary, even though learning has not yet begun.
Predictions are generated using the current state of the model applied to the input features.
A numerical signal is produced to indicate how far the model's current predictions are from the expected outcomes.
Parameter adjustments are calculated based on how a small change would affect the error signal.
The same sequence of operations is executed repeatedly as the model revisits the training data.

rearrange_quiz.validation_text: Well done! You have correctly identified the steps. You can now return to the dashboard to continue with the next exercise.

feedback.general_feedback: When a model uses only linear features (X1, X2), it can combine them only in a linear way. This means it can draw only a straight decision boundary. As a result, only linearly separable datasets can be correctly classified.

options.B: A feature that is created by applying a non-linear transformation to an input

activity_2.instruction: Activity 2 drag and drop: True or False statements

statements.statement: Two clusters can always be separated with a line
statements.feedback: Not quite. Some datasets (circles, spirals) are not linearly separable, so a straight line is not enough.

statements.statement: Hidden layers are required for linear classification
statements.feedback: Incorrect. Linear problems can be solved without hidden layers using a simple linear model.

statements.statement: Logistic regression creates a linear boundary
statements.feedback: Not quite. Logistic regression always produces a linear decision boundary, not non-linear ones.

statements.statement: A neural network without hidden layer behaves like a linear model
statements.feedback: Incorrect. Without hidden layers, a neural network is equivalent to a linear model.

statements.statement: Training is an iterative loop: prediction -> evaluation -> optimization
statements.feedback: Not quite. Training follows this repeating loop, not a single-step process.

statements.statement: when training progresses correctly, loss increases
statements.feedback: Incorrect. If learning works properly, loss should decrease, not increase.

statements.statement: Parameters initialization is the second step of training
statements.feedback: Not quite. Initialization happens first, before any prediction or training begins.

statements.statement: Linear features lead to straight decision boundaries, limiting performance on complex data.
statements.feedback: Incorrect. Linear features can only create straight boundaries, which limits performance on complex data.

statements.statement: Without hidden layers, a model can learn non-linear patterns with non-linear features (e.g., X1², X2²)
statements.feedback: Not quite. Even without hidden layers, non-linear features transform the input space, enabling complex patterns.

exercise_6.title: Exercise #6
exercise_6.visible_parameters: Valider/ modifier les éléments qui apparaissent en vous référant à l'écran de base

instructions.general: In this exercise, you will explore how a neural network builds its prediction step by step. First compare a simple model using only x₁ and x₂ with a model that includes one hidden layer with four neurons.
instructions.activity_1: As seen earlier, it is not possible to classify complex data (such as the two-circle dataset) using linear features. Now try using a hidden layer with four neurons.

pedagogical_overlay.title: Simple model: one equation
pedagogical_overlay.description: This model directly combines x₁ and x₂ using weights and bias. prediction ≈ f(w1·x1 + w2·x2 + b)

pedagogical_overlay.title: Neural Network: What the hidden layer computes
pedagogical_overlay.description: Each neuron combines x₁ and x₂ in a different way, producing 4 new features: a1, a2, a3, a4 with ai = f(wi1·x1 + wi2·x2 + bi). These values are not predictions, they are features learned from the data.

pedagogical_overlay.title: How the full model works
pedagogical_overlay.description: The final prediction is built by combining the learned features. prediction = f(v1·a1 + v2·a2 + v3·a3 + v4·a4 + c)

pedagogical_overlay.title: In Summary
pedagogical_overlay.description: A neural network learns new features using neurons, then combines them to solve more complex problems. (Here, f is an activation function, which determines how each neuron outputs its signal.)

hidden_layer.definition: A hidden layer is a layer of neurons located between the input layer and the output layer in a neural network. Hidden layers allow the network to learn complex patterns and representations from the data.

neuron.definition: A neuron (or node) is a computational unit in a neural network that receives inputs, multiplies them by weights, adds a bias, and applies an activation function to produce an output.

quiz.instruction: Drag and drop True or False?

statements.statement: a hidden neuron creates an intermediate feature, not a final decision
statements.feedback: A hidden neuron produces a new feature from the input data.

statements.statement: The final prediction is computed directly from x₁ and x₂ in all models
statements.feedback: In models with hidden layers, predictions are based on learned features.

statements.statement: A hidden layer allows the network to learn intermediate features.
statements.feedback: hidden layers are where new representations are learned.

statements.statement: Each neuron in a hidden layer learns the same feature.
statements.feedback: different neurons learn different features.

statements.statement: The output of the network combines the features learned by the hidden layer.
statements.feedback: the output uses learned features, not raw inputs.

statements.statement: Adding a hidden layer changes the network from one equation ŷ = f(x₁, x₂) to a composition of equations ŷ = g(f₁(x₁, x₂), ..., f₄(x₁, x₂))
statements.feedback: hidden layers turn the model into a composition of functions, applying activation functions to each step.

statements.statement: Feature learning means manually choosing the right input variables
statements.feedback: feature learning is automatic, not manual.

statements.statement: Feature learning means that a neural network automatically creates new intermediate features from the input data, instead of relying only on the original inputs defined by the user.
statements.feedback: without hidden layers, the model uses a single representation.

exercise_4.visible_parameters: Valider/ modifier les éléments qui apparaissent en vous référant à l'écran de base

instructions.general: In this exercise, you will adjust the bias of a neuron to understand its impact on model performance.
instructions.activity_1: What is the main role of the bias in a neuron?

quiz.question: What is the main role of the bias in a neuron?

options.A: Change the slope of the line
options.B: Shift the line without changing its orientation (true response)

quiz.feedback: The bias plays the role of the intercept: it shifts the decision boundary.

key_idea.title: Key Idea
key_idea.description: The neuron defines a linear decision boundary: w1·x1 + w2·x2 + b = 0. The weights control the orientation of the separating line, while the bias controls the position of the separating line.
points: Weights -> control the orientation of the separating line
Bias -> controls the position of the separating line

exercise_7.title: Exercise #7 Activation Functions
exercise_7.visible_parameters: Valider/ modifier les éléments qui apparaissent en vous référant à l'écran de base

instructions.general: Explore how different activation functions affect the model's behavior and learning.
instructions.activity_1: Test the 4 activation functions: test the model with each activation function, observe what changes after each run, and identify which activation function can classify the dataset (all)

activity_3.instruction: Using the graphical representations of each activation function, and by testing them again in the Playground, drag the properties below into the correct columns

statements.statement: It influences the shape of the decision boundary the model can learn.
statements.feedback_true: Correct. Activation functions affect the kind of boundary the model can represent.
statements.feedback_false: Incorrect. Look at how the decision boundary changes when you switch activation functions.

statements.statement: It changes how each neuron transforms its input before passing it to the next step.
statements.feedback_true: Correct. This is the core role of an activation function.
statements.feedback_false: Incorrect. The activation acts inside each neuron before the signal moves forward.

statements.statement: It changes the bias term, which shifts the decision boundary.
statements.feedback_true: Incorrect. The bias is a parameter learned during training, not changed by the activation.
statements.feedback_false: Correct. Bias shifts the boundary, but activation changes how the signal is transformed.

statements.statement: It changes the values of the weights learned during training.
statements.feedback_true: Incorrect. Weights are updated by training, not directly by the activation function.
statements.feedback_false: Correct. Activation affects the transformation, not the weight values themselves.

activity_3.end_marker: Great! Now let's revisit the definition of an activation function

definition.text: An activation function is a mathematical function applied to the output of a neuron in a neural network. It determines whether the neuron should be activated and what value it should pass to the next layer. More formally, a neuron first computes a weighted sum of its inputs: z = w1·x1 + w2·x2 + ... + b. Where: w = weights, x = input features, b = bias. The activation function f is then applied.
definition.end_marker: Well Done! You have finished this exercise. Go back home to the dashboard, next exercise has been unlocked!

quiz_1.question: What differences do you observe between the two results?

options.feedback: The input features remain the same in both models.

options.text: The training stops earlier in one model
options.feedback: Both models use the same training process.

quiz_1.feedback_correct: That's right! The models use the same data and settings, but their results differ (boundaries and weights).

quiz_2.question: You observed that the decision boundaries are different in each run, even though nothing was changed. What is the main reason?

options.text: Each run starts from a different set of weights
The dataset changes slightly between runs
The initial weights are randomly assigned at the start

quiz_2.feedback_correct: That's correct! Each run starts with randomly initialized weights, so the model begins learning from a different starting point and converges to a different solution (different boundary and final weights).
quiz_2.feedback_incorrect: The dataset does not change. Both models use exactly the same data — the difference comes from how the model is initialized, not from the data itself.

key_idea.title: Key Idea
key_idea.description: A neural network learns by adjusting its weights step by step. If the starting weights are different, the optimization path changes, which leads to different learned patterns, even with the same data and parameters.

activity_1.transition: What conclusions can be drawn from these observations?

low_noise_divergent_model.title: Low noise/divergent model
statements: The error remains constant, preventing the model from improving.
The presence of multiple equivalent minima leads to unstable optimization
The absence of error variation prevents convergence
The weights increase without stabilizing due to repeated updates

high_noise_convergent_model.title: High noise/convergent model
statements: The model converges toward a unique optimal solution
The weights stabilize around an equilibrium value
There is a reachable global minimum error toward which the model can move.
The model eventually stabilizes around an optimal solution, which corresponds to convergence.

activity_2.feedback: When the error remains constant, the model applies the same correction at every step. This repeated update accumulates over time, causing the weights to grow continuously. As a result, the model never stabilizes and diverges instead of reaching a solution. When the error changes, the model adjusts its corrections at each step, making them progressively smaller. This allows the weights to slow down and stabilize instead of increasing continuously. As a result, the model converges toward a stable and optimal solution.

instructions.general: In this exercise, you will review how a neural network learns over time and explore how internal representations are built inside the model.
instructions.secondary: First, let's examine the iterative learning cycle that takes place inside a neural network. You have the option to execute the training incrementally, observing each stage of the process as it unfolds.

steps.title: Step 0 – Initialize the parameters
points: Before training starts, the model does not know anything.
All weights and biases are initialized randomly (small values)
The network has no meaningful representation yet
The decision boundary is random or non-informative
steps.result: The model is ready to start learning, but its predictions are incorrect or arbitrary

steps.title: Step 2 – Compute the error (loss)
points: The model compares its prediction with the true label
If prediction is wrong → error is high
If prediction is close → error is low
steps.result: A single value: the training loss

steps.title: Step 3 – Backward pass (compute corrections)
points: The model determines how to correct its mistake
It computes: 'How much did each weight contribute to the error?'
This uses backpropagation
steps.result: For each weight → a direction and magnitude of update

steps.title: Step 4 – Update the weights
points: The model adjusts its parameters:
New weight = old weight – (learning rate × correction)
Small update → slow but stable learning
Large update → faster but risk of instability

loop_repeat.text: Then the loop repeats from step 1...
points: For many data points
Over many epochs

summary.title: In summary
points: Training is an iterative loop: predict → measure error → correct → update
Each step slightly improves the model
Learning emerges progressively over many iterations
summary.note: You can run the model again to observe these steps in action; Whenever you are ready click 'Next' to proceed to the next activity.

activity_1.instruction: Match each dataset type with its specificities

training_data: (1) The model directly updates its weights using this data
(2) The loss on this data decreases continuously during training
(7) This dataset is seen by the model during backpropagation
(5) The model can memorize patterns specific to this data
(8) Performance on this data may become misleadingly good (overfitting)
test_data: (3) This dataset remains unseen during weight updates
(4) The model does not learn directly from this data
(6) Overfitting is observed when performance worsens on this data
(9) This data reflects how well the model performs on new, unseen inputs
(10) This data is used to evaluate generalization performance

activity_1.transition: Now that you have identified the roles of training data and test data, let's see how this translates in practice. Run the model with the given configuration and observe how the training loss and test loss evolve during training. Pay close attention to what this reveals about the model's ability to generalize.

activity_2.instruction: Did you observe the following items ? (if not, reset and run the model again)

checklist.observation: Evolution of the training loss over time (speed and stability)
checklist.explanation: → The training loss should decrease steadily as the model learns patterns from the training data.

checklist.observation: Evolution of the test loss over time (level and fluctuations)
checklist.explanation: → The test loss may decrease initially but can stabilize or increase if the model fails to generalize.

checklist.observation: Gap between training and test loss and whether it increases
checklist.explanation: → An increasing gap indicates the model is fitting the training data better than the test data.

checklist.observation: Moment when the two curves start to diverge
checklist.explanation: → The point where test loss starts increasing while training loss keeps decreasing signals overfitting.

checklist.observation: Signs of overfitting (training improves while test worsens)
checklist.explanation: → Overfitting occurs when performance improves on training data but degrades on test data.

checklist.observation: Overall generalization performance on unseen data
checklist.explanation: → Good generalization means similar performance on both training and test data.

checklist.observation: Amount of training data available (here very limited – 10%)
checklist.explanation: → With only 10% training data, the model has limited examples to learn general patterns.

checklist.observation: Evidence of memorization of training data (rapid loss decrease)
checklist.explanation: → A very fast decrease in training loss suggests the model is memorizing rather than learning.

checklist.observation: Difficulty to generalize from few examples
checklist.explanation: → With few examples, the model struggles to apply learned patterns to new data.

checklist.observation: Impact of noise and lack of data on model behavior
checklist.explanation: → Noise and insufficient data increase the risk of learning irrelevant or misleading patterns.

activity_2.key_insight: Overfitting can result from both model complexity and insufficient training data

instructions.general: Explore how increasing the learning rate affects training stability on a separable dataset using a logistic regression model.
instructions.activity_1: Test the different learning rates. Run the model for each learning rate and assess whether it converges or diverges. Use up to 3000 epochs if needed. Pause the model once you can determine the outcome, Remember to reset it before each new run!

statements.statement: A separable dataset allows logistic regression to converge even with relatively large learning rates.
statements.feedback_true: Correct. On separable data, logistic regression can remain stable even with relatively high learning rates.
statements.feedback_false: Incorrect. In this exercise, the model can still converge with large learning rates because the dataset is separable and the optimization is well-behaved.

statements.statement: The loss in logistic regression on separable data remains well-behaved, which prevents divergence for a wide range of learning rates.
statements.feedback_true: Correct. The loss is well-conditioned in this setting, which helps the model stay stable across many learning rates.
statements.feedback_false: Incorrect. In this exercise, the loss landscape remains stable enough to avoid divergence for many learning rates.

statements.statement: A high learning rate always causes divergence, even for simple models like logistic regression.
statements.feedback_true: Incorrect. A high learning rate does not always cause divergence. In simple cases like logistic regression on separable data, the model can still converge.
statements.feedback_false: Correct. A high learning rate can cause divergence in some cases, but not always. In this exercise, logistic regression on separable data can tolerate high values without diverging.

activity_3.general_conclusion: The learning rate impacts the stability of training: if it is too high, it can cause divergence due to large and unstable updates, while lower values promote stable convergence. However, this effect depends on the model and the data: simple models like logistic regression on separable datasets can tolerate much higher learning rates without diverging, unlike more complex neural networks

instructions.general: In this exercise, you will explore how the choice of activation function affects learning in a deep neural network and influences gradient propagation.
instructions.secondary: First, let's examine the definition of a gradient in a Neural Network

definition.title: What is a gradient?
definition.text: A gradient is the signal used to update the model during learning.
how_it_works: The gradient tells how to change each weight to reduce this error

key_idea.text: The gradient improves parameter with both Direction (where to go) and Magnitude (how big the change should be).
points: Large gradient — big update
Small gradient — tiny update

activity_1.instruction: Run both models until they reach a stable state. Focus closely on weights and neurons during this process.

sigmoid.weight_updates: Very small updates in early layers
sigmoid.neuron_feature_learning: Early neurons fail to learn useful features

activity_2.instruction: Identify the correct conclusions. For each pair, select the correct statement

quiz.correct_statement: The neurons and weights in the first layers barely changed because the error signal (backward pass) did not reach them.
quiz.incorrect_statement: The neurons and weights in the first layers changed very slowly because most of the learning was concentrated in the deeper layers.

quiz.correct_statement: The gradient, which is responsible for updating the weights and enabling learning, becomes smaller and eventually disappears.
quiz.incorrect_statement: The gradient becomes very stable at small values, allowing the model to converge smoothly without large weight updates.

quiz.correct_statement: The Sigmoid function is responsible for the gradient killing phenomenon because it strongly reduces the gradient at each layer.
quiz.incorrect_statement: The gradient killing phenomenon mainly occurs when the model is too deep, regardless of the activation function used.

activity_2.transition: Great! Let's finish with a Find the Mistake game

relu.title: 3.a. ReLU activation Function
relu.description: With ReLU transformation only two possible gradient values: 1 when the neuron is active (x > 0) and 0 when the neuron is inactive (x ≤ 0). ReLU does NOT shrink gradients (no multiplication by small values). When active → gradient stays strong (1) → learning continues.

details.gradient_0: No signal passes. No learning for that neuron ("dead neuron").
details.gradient_1: Full signal passes backward. Weights are updated normally.

sigmoid.title: 3.b. Sigmoïd activation Function
sigmoid.description: Sigmoid derivative is always ≤ 0.25. Chain effect in deep networks means gradient ≈ 0.25 * 0.25 * 0.25 * ... This leads to extremely small gradients (e.g. for 6 layers, 0.25^6 ≈ 0.00024), which is known as "gradient killing". It gets "killed" during backpropagation.

quiz.statement: The gradient becomes almost infinite after multiplication.
quiz.hint_reveal: Give me a Hint / Reveal the answer
quiz.feedback: Correct! The gradient becomes almost zero, not infinite. This happens because multiplying many small derivatives (Sigmoid) makes the gradient vanish, which stops learning.

activity_2.title: 2 - How do you think the activation function changes the way the model works?

statements.statement: It changes the bias term, which shifts the decision boundary.
statements.feedback_true: ❌ Incorrect. The bias is a parameter learned during training, not changed by the activation.
statements.feedback_false: ✅ Correct. Bias shifts the boundary, but activation changes how the signal is transformed.

statements.statement: It influences the shape of the decision boundary the model can learn.
statements.feedback_true: ✅ Correct. Activation functions affect the kind of boundary the model can represent.
statements.feedback_false: ❌ Incorrect. Look at how the decision boundary changes when you switch activation functions.

statements.statement: It changes how each neuron transforms its input before passing it to the next step
statements.feedback_true: ✅ Correct. This is the core role of an activation function.
statements.feedback_false: ❌ Incorrect. The activation acts inside each neuron before the signal moves forward.

statements.statement: It changes the values of the weights learned during training.
statements.feedback_true: ❌ Incorrect. Weights are updated by training, not directly by the activation function.
statements.feedback_false: ✅ Correct. Activation affects the transformation, not the weight values themselves.
